section_1.title: Prerequisites: The Geometry of Complex Numbers
section_1.content: Briefly review the complex plane (Argand diagram). Explain that a 2D equation f(z) = w is essentially a transformation of the plane. Use a 'Rubber Sheet' metaphor: imagine the input grid being warped and folded by a function.
section_1.example: A grid of squares transforming into a swirling vortex pattern when f(z) = z².

section_2.title: Numerical Root Finding in 2D
section_2.content: Introduce the Newton-Raphson method extended to 2D complex numbers. Instead of scalar lines, we look for points where the magnitude |f(z)| = 0. We visualize the basins of attraction for different roots.
section_2.example: A 'Robot Scout' navigating a landscape of mountains (high values) to find the valley (zero/root) using a gradient descent path.

section_3.title: Decoding the Winding Number
section_3.content: Define the Winding Number as how many times a curve wraps around the origin. Explain that it is a topological 'fingerprint' of how many roots are enclosed within a loop. Connect this to the Argument Principle.
section_3.example: A 'Digital Lasso' circling a region; the number of times the rope wraps around a target 'Treasure' (the root) equals the winding number.

section_4.title: Domain Coloring: The Visual Language of Functions
section_4.content: Explain how to map 2D complex outputs to color space (Hue for argument/angle, Brightness/Saturation for magnitude). This turns abstract algebra into a continuous, navigable terrain.
section_4.example: A 'Color-Coded Weather Map' where specific colors signify phases and intensity levels, revealing zeros as 'black holes' where all colors converge.

section_5.title: Synthesis: Solving Equations Visually
section_5.content: Synthesize the concepts: Use domain coloring to spot potential zeros, then apply numerical solvers, and verify counts using the winding number. Conclude with the power of visual computation.
section_5.example: An 'Explorer's HUD' displaying a domain-colored map, using a winding number scanner to count hidden roots, and triggering a numerical solver to pinpoint them exactly.
